title: Impact of Catalytic Converter Mandate on NOx Emissions

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
Difference-in-Differences (DID) is the appropriate method here since we have treatment and control regions observed before and after the catalytic converter mandate implementation. The key assumption is parallel trends: absent the mandate, treated and control regions would have followed similar trends in NOx emissions. The interaction term `treat_x_post` captures the causal effect of the mandate.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load required libraries
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(fixest)
library(ggplot2)

# Read the data
data <- read_csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s47_data.csv")

# Main DID regression with unit and time fixed effects
did_model <- feols(y ~ treat_x_post | unit_id + period, data = data)

# Print main result
cat("Main DID Result:\n")
cat("Effect of Catalytic Converter Mandate on Log NOx Emissions:\n")
cat("Coefficient:", round(coef(did_model)["treat_x_post"], 4), "\n")
cat("Standard Error:", round(se(did_model)["treat_x_post"], 4), "\n")
cat("P-value:", round(pvalue(did_model)["treat_x_post"], 4), "\n")

# Create summary table
summary(did_model)

# Robustness Check 1: Simple DID without fixed effects
simple_did <- lm(y ~ treated + post + treat_x_post, data = data)
cat("\nRobustness Check 1 - Simple DID (no fixed effects):\n")
cat("Coefficient:", round(coef(simple_did)["treat_x_post"], 4), "\n")

# Robustness Check 2: Check parallel trends assumption
# Calculate pre-treatment means by group and period
pre_treatment <- data %>%
  filter(post == 0) %>%
  group_by(period, treated) %>%
  summarise(mean_y = mean(y), .groups = 'drop')

# Visual check of parallel trends
ggplot(pre_treatment, aes(x = period, y = mean_y, color = factor(treated))) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Pre-treatment Trends Check",
       x = "Period", 
       y = "Mean Log NOx Emissions",
       color = "Treated") +
  theme_minimal()

# Robustness Check 3: Placebo test with lagged treatment
# Create placebo treatment one period earlier
data_placebo <- data %>%
  mutate(placebo_post = ifelse(period >= max(period[post == 1]) - 1, 1, 0),
         placebo_interact = treated * placebo_post) %>%
  filter(post == 0)  # Only use pre-treatment periods

if(nrow(data_placebo) > 0) {
  placebo_model <- feols(y ~ placebo_interact | unit_id + period, data = data_placebo)
  cat("\nRobustness Check 3 - Placebo Test:\n")
  cat("Placebo Coefficient:", round(coef(placebo_model)["placebo_interact"], 4), "\n")
  cat("Placebo P-value:", round(pvalue(placebo_model)["placebo_interact"], 4), "\n")
}

# Summary statistics by treatment status and time
cat("\nSummary Statistics:\n")
summary_stats <- data %>%
  group_by(treated, post) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_y = round(mean(y), 4),
    sd_y = round(sd(y), 4),
    .groups = 'drop'
  )
print(summary_stats)
```

## 3. Expected Findings
I expect a negative coefficient (around -0.3 to -0.8) indicating that the catalytic converter mandate significantly reduces NOx emissions. Environmental regulations like catalytic converter mandates are specifically designed to reduce harmful emissions, and the technology is well-established for NOx reduction. The magnitude should be economically meaningful given that this is measured in log terms, representing a percentage reduction in emissions levels.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Compare changes in log NOx emissions between treated and untreated regions over time.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The catalytic converter mandate significantly reduces log NOx emissions.
